say: Today you are turtle pilots. A turtle with a pen can draw any shape, but only if you tell it exactly how far to turn at every corner.
Our rule today: work the turn out with maths first, then test it in code. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Stand up, or sit and use your arm as the turtle’s nose, and face your screen. Call that north. I am the programmer and you are the turtle. Turn right 90. Which way are you facing now?
Now: how can you make one full turn using 3 equal turns? How big is each turn?
Here is the square program: repeat 4, move 100, turn right 90. I want an equilateral triangle. What turn should I type? Write your prediction on your whiteboard before anyone runs it.
stuck: Stuck: walk the shape yourself. Walk one side, then turn at the corner. How far did your body turn?
Typed turn 60 for the triangle? Run it and look. Does the turtle come home? How far has it turned altogether?
Finished early: the pentagon (the Go further what-if), then predict the turn for a regular shape with 10 sides and test it.

say: “An octagon has 8 equal turns. To come home facing the same way the turtle turns 360° altogether, so each turn is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. The turn and the inside angle sit on one straight line, so the inside angle is 180 − 45 = 135°.”
“Working backwards: the inside angle is 174°, so the turn is 180 − 174 = 6°. The turns make 360°, so there are 360 ÷ 6 = 60 sides.”
“For the star the turtle goes round twice: 720° altogether. 5 equal turns: 720 ÷ 5 = 144°. The angle at each point is 180 − 144 = 36°.”

do: Ask: “What did you predict before you ran it? Were you right?”
Ask: “How far has your turtle turned altogether? How do you know?”
Ask: “Which angle does the turtle turn: the inside angle or the outside one? Show me on the picture.”
stuck: Hint 1: “To come home facing the same way, the turtle makes one full turn: 360°.”
Hint 2: “The corners are equal, so share 360° equally between them.”
Hint 3: “The turn and the inside angle sit on one straight line: they add up to 180°.”

say: “Ali says the turtle turns by the inside angle of the shape. Mei says it turns by the outside angle. Who is right? Use a triangle to explain.”
ask: “Ali says the turtle turns by the inside angle of the shape. Mei says it turns by the outside angle. Who is right? Use a triangle to explain.”

Mei is right. For an equilateral triangle the inside angle is 60° but the turtle turns 120°; turning 60° three times only draws half a hexagon. The turtle starts facing one way and comes home facing the same way after going round once, so it has made exactly one full turn: 360°. A star goes round more than once, so its turns add up to 720°, 1080° and so on.

say: “Today you predicted every turn with maths and then tested it in code. That is how mathematicians and programmers work together. Well done, inquirers!”

p6l7-title.note: Objective: Use the idea that a turtle going once round a closed shape turns 360° altogether to find the turn angle (360° ÷ sides) and inside angle (180° − turn) of regular polygons, work backwards from an angle to the number of sides, extend to star polygons (turn = 360° × times round ÷ points), and test every prediction with a pen program in Scratch (or Python turtle). Materials: A laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 open (scratch.mit.edu) and the Pen extension added (starter file L7_Turtle_Start.sb3), mini whiteboards, a protractor, plain or squared paper. Online: The tutor shares the starter file L7_Turtle_Start.sb3 (Pen extension already added and the 4 set-up blocks already in place) through the approved channel, so children only open it (File, Load from your computer; no account needed). Pairs work in breakout rooms: one child drives Scratch and shares the screen, the other predicts, then they swap. Children describe their drawings aloud. A tablet works for Scratch but is slower. Every drawing starts with the same 4 set-up blocks (erase all, go to x: -50 y: 100, point in direction 90, pen down) so shapes stay on the stage; turn blocks in Scratch show an arrow (turn ↻ is clockwise, our “turn right”). Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left (Motion, Pen, Control), not by colour. Scratch set-up: before the lesson, check every child can open scratch.mit.edu and add the Pen extension (the button at the bottom left of the block menu). The turtle is any sprite with its pen down; in Scratch the turn block is "turn ↻ … degrees" (clockwise), shown on our slides as "turn right". Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5, warm-up 6.5 to 13, explore at the computer 13 to 27.5, mini-lesson 27.5 to 40 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 40 to 45.5, worksheet 45.5 to 75.5 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 75.5 to 78 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 78 to 83, exit slip 83 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90.

p6l7-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: Facing the door again. Four quarter turns make one full turn (4 × 90° = 360°). Children who cannot stand can use an arm or a drawing of an arrow. Puzzle 2: 9 corners. The turtle turns 360° altogether and each turn is 40°, so 360 ÷ 40 = 9. A guess is welcome. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l7-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 10.5. Turtle says (the game stays about 150 seconds; if you run late stop after call 4). Everyone stands (online: stand back from the camera) or sits and uses an arm as the turtle’s nose; nobody has to stand. The turns follow on from each other: each one starts where the last one ended. Call each turn, children turn their bodies, then ask "Which way are you facing?" and click to show it. 1) right 90 from north: east. 2) right 180 from east: west. 3) left 270 from west: north (left 270 is the same as right 90). 4) right 45: north-east. 5) right 360: a full turn, still north-east. 6) "Make one full turn in 3 equal turns. How big is each?" 360 ÷ 3 = 120°. Ask: "Which other turn would have done the same as left 270?" (right 90). Keep this picture in mind: a full turn is 360°.

p6l7-warm2.note: Minutes 10.5 to 13. Three questions only. Read each aloud, give thinking time, take answers on whiteboards, then click. Ask "How do you know?" each time. 1) 360°. 2) 180 − 50 − 75 = 55°. 3) 45. These facts (straight line 180°, full turn 360°) are the two tools for today.

p6l7-explore1.note: Minutes 13 to 27.5 (this slide 13 to 18). The Set-up slide is merged into this one. The Turtle start file (L7_Turtle_Start.sb3, sent to families with the workbook; the tutor also keeps a copy) already has the 4 set-up blocks (erase all, go to x: -50 y: 100, point in direction 90, pen down), so children open it in about 60 seconds instead of building them; a child without the file adds the Pen extension (blue button, bottom left) and builds the 4 blocks. Say the stage size aloud: 480 wide, 360 tall, shapes grow right and DOWN; start at x: -50, y: 100 so every shape stays on the stage (up to 10 sides move 80, 12 to 15 sides move 50, 24 sides move 30, 36 sides move 10). Turn ↻ is clockwise, our turn right. One child drives Scratch, the other predicts the turn BEFORE each run; swap for each shape. Build the square program together first and run it. Then the challenge: change one number to get an equilateral triangle. Expect many pairs to type 60 (the inside angle): let them run it. It draws only half a hexagon. Ask: "How far did the turtle turn altogether? Did it come home?" Then the hexagon only (6 sides); the pentagon (5 sides, turn 72) is the Go further what-if. If a pair wants more: the pentagon, then a regular shape with 10 sides. Online: breakout rooms, the driver shares their screen. Every run starts with the same 4 set-up blocks (erase all, go to x: -50 y: 100, point in direction 90, pen down) so each run starts clean and stays on the stage. Pairs add the other blocks below them. Use the clockwise arrow turn block. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if you want a regular PENTAGON (5 sides)? Predict the turn, then test it in Scratch with repeat 5. What about 10 sides? Answer: 72° for 5 sides (360 ÷ 5) and 36° for 10 sides (360 ÷ 10).

p6l7-explore2.note: Minutes 18 to 27.5. Two questions (1 and 3). Let pairs finish, then gather. Answers: 1) 120°. Turn 60 draws only half a hexagon: 3 × 60 = 180°, so the turtle does not come home. 2) 360°: the turtle comes home facing the same way, so it has made one full turn. Collect the table on the board: 3 sides 120°, 4 sides 90°, 5 sides 72°, 6 sides 60°, and multiply each pair. Do not name the rule yet: the teaching slides do that.

p6l7-teach1.note: Minutes 27.5 to 29. Teach. Act it out: walk along a line on the floor, stop at the "corner" and point straight on, then turn to face the new side. "How far did I turn? Not the angle inside the corner: the angle from straight on." Click 1: the walk. Click 2: the turn (red). Click 3: the inside angle (teal): angles on a straight line make 180°. Click 4: the big idea. Think-aloud: "In Explore the square needed 90 and the triangle needed 120, not 60. That is because the turtle turns the outside angle. Every time it comes home facing the way it started, it has turned exactly once round: 360°. Sides times turn was 360 every time."

p6l7-we1.note:
Minutes 29 to 31. Click through the steps; ask the group to predict each before you reveal it. Think-aloud: "An octagon has 8 equal turns. To come home facing the same way the turtle turns 360° altogether, so each turn is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. The turn and the inside angle sit on one straight line, so the inside angle is 180 − 45 = 135°." Step 4: build it live in Scratch and run it. Ask: "What would 8 turns of 135 draw?" (try it: it does not close after 8, because 8 × 135 = 1080, 3 times round, and it draws an 8-point star: a preview of the star slide). Optional Python version (Python turtle module; it opens a drawing window), for children who already know Python:
import turtle
t = turtle.Turtle()
n, k = 5, 2 # points, rounds
turn = 360 * k / n
for i in range(n):
 t.forward(150)
 t.right(turn)
print(turn, n * turn)
turtle.done()
Run as it is, it draws the 5-point star and prints 144.0 720.0 (the turn, then the total turning). Change n and k: n, k = 8, 1 draws the octagon and prints 45.0 360.0.

p6l7-try1.note: Minutes 31 to 32.5. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) 360 ÷ 20 = 18°. b) 180 − 18 = 162°. c) 360 ÷ 360 = 1°, inside 179°: with tiny steps (move 1) it looks just like a circle. That is how Scratch artists draw circles: repeat 360 [move 1, turn right 1]. Let a fast pair test it.

p6l7-we2.note: Minutes 32.5 to 34.5. Click through. Think-aloud: "Working backwards: the inside angle is 174°, so the turn is 180 − 174 = 6°. The turns make 360°, so there are 360 ÷ 6 = 60 sides." The last box is the important twist: a turn angle must share 360 exactly. Ask: "Could a regular polygon have a turn of 7°?" (no: 360 ÷ 7 is not whole). "Which whole-number turns work?" (the factors of 360 that are less than 180: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40, 45, 60, 72, 90, 120).

p6l7-try2.note: Minutes 34.5 to 36. Whiteboards, then click. a) 360 ÷ 4 = 90. b) turn 180 − 168 = 12°, 360 ÷ 12 = 30. c) The turn would be 55°, and 360 ÷ 55 = 6.54…, not a whole number of sides. Ask a child to explain c in words.

p6l7-we3.note: Minutes 36 to 38.5. Ask first: "The pentagon was repeat 5, turn 72. What happens if I double the turn to 144?" Take predictions, then click through. Think-aloud: "For the star the turtle goes round twice: 720° altogether. 5 equal turns: 720 ÷ 5 = 144°. The angle at each point is 180 − 144 = 36°." Last click: run it in Scratch (after the 4 set-up blocks) and show the star. Point out: the turtle still turns at 5 corners, but it goes round twice, so the turns add up to 720°, not 360°. The angle at each point is still on a straight line with the turn: 180 − 144 = 36°. Ask: "How many times round would a turn of 216 go?" (5 × 216 = 1080: 3 times; it is the same star drawn the other way round).

p6l7-key.note: Minutes 38.5 to 40. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Using the inside angle as the turn: turn 60° for a triangle draws half a hexagon, and turn 108° for a pentagon does not close. (2) Dividing 180 by the number of sides instead of 360, or forgetting that turn + inside angle = 180°. (3) Stars: thinking the turns always add up to 360°. A star goes round more than once, so its turns add up to 720°, 1080° and so on.

p6l7-break.note: Minutes 40 to 45.5. 5.5 minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and turn on the spot. Ask during the hexagon: "How big is each turn?" (60°, a sixth of a turn).

p6l7-ws1.note: Minutes 45.5 to 55.5. At the computer in pairs. Walk around. Ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. For Q2 insist on a written prediction before anyone runs the program.

p6l7-ws1ans.note: Minutes 55.5 to 58.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q1 (the backwards rows), about 35 seconds a question. Q1: the backwards rows: 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides, 180 − 24 = 156°; 180 − 165 = 15°, 360 ÷ 15 = 24 sides. Q2: 120 is the turn of a triangle, so after 3 moves the turtle is home, and the other 6 moves go round the same triangle twice more. Run it slowly in Scratch (add "wait 0.5 seconds" inside the loop) so children see it.

p6l7-teachtrace.note: Minutes 58.5 to 61. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 traces a different star). Click to add each row while children say the next total. A trace table is how programmers check code by hand: one row for each time round the loop. Ask: "How do we know how many times the turtle went round?" (divide the total by 360).

p6l7-teachstar.note: Minutes 61 to 63.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 plans two different stars). Click through the steps, then the picture. Say the order out loud: times round → total turning → turn → point angle. Ask: "Which star has sharper points, this one or the 5-point star?" (the 5-point star: 36° is smaller than 45°).

p6l7-ws2.note: Minutes 63.5 to 72.5. Children work alone on Q3 and Q4 (they may test in Scratch); Q5 (inside-angle sums) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson.

p6l7-ws2ans.note: Minutes 72.5 to 75.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q3 (the running total). Q5 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson (the octagon idea: every corner gives a straight line of 180°, the turns make 360°, so the inside angles add up to n × 180° − 360°). Q4: the 9-point star has the sharper points (20°). Q5: each inside angle 60, 90, 108, 120, 144; the rule can also be written n × 180 − 360 (the turtle way). Ask: "Why does one more side add 180°?" (one more corner adds one more straight line of 180°, and the turns still make 360°).

p6l7-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. For children who finish early (not on the worksheet). Answers: 1) A square (turn = inside = 90°, because they add up to 180°) 2) 10, 12, 15, 18 and 20 sides (turns 36°, 30°, 24°, 20°, 18°); 360 cannot be shared exactly into 11, 13, 14, 16, 17 or 19 equal turns 3) Three hexagon angles make 3 × 120° = 360°. Pentagons cannot: 3 × 108° = 324° leaves a gap and 4 × 108° = 432° overlaps.

p6l7-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first (they may test ideas in Scratch), then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. Answers: 1) No: 5 × 108° = 540° is not a whole number of turns. 108 × 10 = 1080 = 3 × 360, so 10 repeats close it: a 10-point star that goes round 3 times (each point 72°). 2) Only 1: turn 150°, going round 5 times (5 × 360 ÷ 12). Turns 60°, 90° and 120° (round 2, 3, 4 times) just redraw a hexagon, square or triangle, and 180° goes back and forth on a line.

p6l7-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Q1: "Where would the turtle have to be to close the shape? How many more turns of 108 until the total is a whole number of full turns?" Q2: a star with 12 points joins every k-th dot, and the turn is 30° × k. "Join every 2nd dot. Every 3rd. Which jumps visit all 12 dots?"

p6l7-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: list the multiples of 108 until one is a multiple of 360 (1080 = 3 × 360). Test it in Scratch: repeat 10 [move 150, turn right 108] draws a 10-point star. Q2: a jump that shares a factor with 12 (2, 3, 4, 6) gets back to 0 early and redraws a smaller shape; only jumps 1 and 5 (and 7 and 11, which are the same shapes the other way round) visit all 12 dots, and jump 1 is the 12-gon. Link to Q4 on the worksheet.

p6l7-talk.note: Minutes 78 to 83. One question only. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then volunteers share. Second question (only if flex is left; otherwise the opener of the next lesson): Why do the turns add up to 360° for every shape the turtle draws going round once?” (Only if flex is left; otherwise it is the opener of the next lesson.) Answer: Mei is right. For an equilateral triangle the inside angle is 60° but the turtle turns 120°; turning 60° three times only draws half a hexagon. The turtle starts facing one way and comes home facing the same way after going round once, so it has made exactly one full turn: 360°. A star goes round more than once, so its turns add up to 720°, 1080° and so on. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

p6l7-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86. Answer: 72 sides (360 ÷ 5 = 72); each inside angle is 175° (180 − 5). Children who write 175 sides and 5° have swapped the two steps: ask "Which angle does the turtle turn?" Extension: Draw a rosette: repeat 12 [draw a square, then turn ↻ 30]. Start this one with go to x: 0 y: 0 instead of x: -50 y: 100, so the rosette stays on the stage. How far does the turtle turn altogether? (12 × (360 + 30) = 4680° = 13 full turns.) Design your own rosette and predict its total turning before you run it.

p6l7-reflect.note: Minutes 86 to 88. Looking back is 2 full minutes, after the exit slip, and is never shortened. Everyone has the box: it is on the Finish page, a page every child reaches. Say: "Two minutes, just for you. Finish: something I did well, the hardest part was, and tick what helped. You can write pass. If you are still stuck, tick that box and I will check in with you in the open session, in the shared room, with your parent nearby." Never collect it in front of the group and never read an answer out. Never ask a child to show the box to the camera; a child who ticks “I am still stuck” is followed up after class through the parent. Praise the strategy, not the speed: say "you added up the turns, and that is what got you unstuck", never "you were quick". If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session the same day: visit the shared breakout room or use a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never by private message. If a child writes "everything" or "I am bad at maths", say quietly in the open session: "Thank you for telling me. Let's find one small thing that worked today," and point to a specific item they got right. If a child writes that nothing was hard, ask what would make it harder.
